summary_html: A **court reverses or vacates** a CPS or agency decision due to procedural error, insufficient evidence, or constitutional violation. Federal review data (CFSR, ASFA) tracks judicial determinations on reasonable efforts and due process.
authority_html:
- **Adoption and Safe Families Act (ASFA)** — judicial findings of 'reasonable efforts' compliance  
- **CFSR Regulations (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal review of judicial/agency conformity  
- **42 U.S.C. § 1983** — civil-rights remedy for unconstitutional removals (14th & 4th Amendments).

provisions_triggered.name: Due Process / Law of the Land

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: Due process and due course of law require an appellate court to review and detail its analysis of endangerment findings under § 161.001(b)(1)(D) or (E), because those findings can ground a future termination as to other children.
key_cases.relevance: A Texas appellate court commits reversible error if it declines to reach (D) and (E) findings; this is the most frequently invoked reversal ground in current Texas termination appeals.
key_cases.quote: We hold that due process and due course of law requirements mandate that an appellate court detail its analysis for an appeal of termination of parental rights

key_cases.holding: Evidence of a decades-old offense and a deportation, with no service plan ever offered and no evidence of endangering conduct, is legally insufficient to terminate a father's rights.
key_cases.relevance: The leading modern Texas reversal for legally insufficient endangerment evidence.
key_cases.quote: We conclude the evidence is legally insufficient and, accordingly, reverse the court of appeals

key_cases.holding: Factual sufficiency review in a termination case asks whether the evidence would permit a factfinder reasonably to form a firm belief or conviction about the truth of the State's allegations.
key_cases.relevance: The Texas factual-sufficiency standard an appellate court uses when it reverses a trial court's termination or conservatorship findings.
key_cases.quote: whether the evidence is such that a fact-finder could reasonably form a firm belief or conviction

key_cases.holding: An ineffective-assistance claim survives the failure to file a statement of appellate points, and former § 263.405(i) is unconstitutional as applied where it would bar review of a meritorious sufficiency complaint.
key_cases.relevance: Removes the procedural trap that had been defeating Texas termination appeals, and is the authority for reaching the merits when trial counsel defaulted.
key_cases.quote: an ineffective assistance of counsel claim can be raised on appeal despite the failure to include it in a statement of points

key_cases.holding: The statutory right to appointed counsel in a parental-rights termination case includes the right to effective assistance, measured by the Strickland standard.
key_cases.relevance: The basis on which a Texas termination judgment is set aside for counsel's failure — here, failure to preserve a factual sufficiency complaint.
key_cases.quote: We hold that the statutory right to counsel in parental-rights termination cases embodies the right to effective counsel

key_cases.case_name: Gates v. Texas Department of Family & Protective Services
key_cases.court: Court of Appeals of Texas, Third District (Austin)
key_cases.holding: A person named in a central-registry abuse finding need not exhaust the Department's administrative review (ARIF, then Office of Consumer Affairs or SOAH) before suing in district court, because Family Code § 261.309 makes that remedy non-exclusive.
key_cases.relevance: Establishes the judicial route by which an agency abuse finding is set aside in Texas.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that the legislature has not vested exclusive jurisdiction over such complaints in the Department

key_cases.holding: Only a trial court's failure to extend the Family Code § 263.401 automatic dismissal date before that date passes is jurisdictional; every other claimed defect in complying with § 263.401(b) is non-jurisdictional and must be preserved for appellate review. A docket-sheet pronouncement sufficed to extend the date here, so the final decree was not void.
key_cases.relevance: The reversal route the court of appeals took here (declaring the decree void) is the one G.X.H. rejects for non-jurisdictional § 263.401(b) defects; an appellate attack on the deadline now turns on preservation.
key_cases.quote: The Legislature’s 2017 amendments changed the consequence of expiration of the statutory deadline (without an extension or commencement of the trial) so that it is now jurisdictional.

key_cases.holding: Only one predicate ground under Family Code § 161.001(1), plus a best-interest finding, is needed to support termination; and subsection (Q), which permits termination where a parent will be imprisoned and unable to care for the child for two years, operates prospectively and is constitutional as applied to a parent imprisoned before its effective date.
key_cases.relevance: Explains why a reviewing court may affirm without reaching the remaining grounds, and therefore why a parent challenging sufficiency must knock out all of them — the structural reason most sufficiency reversals fail.
key_cases.quote: Only one predicate finding under section 161.001(1) is necessary to support a judgment of termination when there is also a finding that termination is in the child’s best interest.

key_cases.case_name: Texas Department of Human Services v. E.B.
key_cases.holding: In a jury trial to terminate parental rights the controlling question is whether the parent-child relationship should be terminated, and Rule 277 requires that question to be submitted in broad form with the statutory endangerment grounds given as instructions; submitting a single broad-form question covering two independent grounds was not an abuse of discretion.
key_cases.relevance: The broad-form rule is the foundation In re B.L.D. builds on and the reason charge complaints in termination appeals are reviewed for abuse of discretion rather than as a matter of right.
key_cases.quote: Unless extraordinary circumstances exist, a court must submit such broad-form questions.

key_cases.holding: A court of appeals conducting a factual-sufficiency review of a termination must consider the entire record, but it is required to detail the evidence and explain the insufficiency only when it reverses the factfinder; it need not detail the evidence when it affirms.
key_cases.relevance: Defines the deference an appellate court owes the factfinder on factual sufficiency and the asymmetric duty to write — detail required to reverse, not to affirm. It is the companion to In re C.H. and the answer to a parent's argument that a short affirmance shows no real review occurred.
key_cases.quote: Thus, if the reviewing court is to reverse the factfinder, it must detail the evidence supporting its decision.

key_cases.holding: On legal-sufficiency review of a clear-and-convincing termination finding the court considers all the evidence, not only the evidence favoring the verdict; it disregards contrary evidence a reasonable factfinder could have disbelieved but may not disregard undisputed contrary facts.
key_cases.relevance: Completes the Texas sufficiency trio with In re J.F.C. and In re A.C. by stating the no-evidence standard for a clear-and-convincing finding, including the limit that undisputed contrary facts cannot be ignored.
key_cases.quote: Therefore, in conducting a legal sufficiency review in a parental termination case, we must consider all of the evidence, not just that which favors the verdict.

key_cases.holding: A parent who opposes a government-initiated termination suit may raise ineffective assistance of counsel on appeal whether counsel was appointed or privately retained; on this record, however, the mother could not show deficient performance under Strickland, so the judgment was affirmed.
key_cases.relevance: Supplies the appellate vehicle for attacking a termination through counsel's performance, and makes clear the claim is still tested under Strickland, so the reversal rate remains low.
key_cases.quote: parents may assert a claim for ineffective assistance of counsel, regardless of whether counsel is retained or appointed

key_cases.holding: The statutory right of an indigent parent to appointed counsel under Family Code § 107.013(a)(1) runs through the exhaustion of appeals under § 107.016(2)(B) and therefore includes proceedings in the Supreme Court of Texas, including the petition for review; appointed counsel may satisfy that duty with an Anders-standard petition.
key_cases.relevance: The practical completion of In re M.S. — a parent whose appointed lawyer is allowed to withdraw after the court of appeals is entitled to new counsel, not to a dead-ended appeal.
key_cases.quote: we hold that the right to counsel under Section 107.013(a)(1) through the exhaustion of appeals under Section 107.016(2)(B) includes all proceedings in this Court

key_cases.holding: An inmate has no absolute right to appear in person in a civil proceeding; the burden is on the inmate to identify, in the bench-warrant request, the facts showing why his personal appearance is necessary, and a trial court that proceeds without ruling on a request containing no such information does not abuse its discretion.
key_cases.relevance: Forecloses the most common appellate complaint from an absent incarcerated parent unless the bench-warrant request itself laid out the necessity factors.
key_cases.quote: However, an inmate does not have an absolute right to appear in person in every court proceeding.
